per_question.question: Lambda SnapStart and provisioned concurrency both exist to reduce cold-start latency, but you can't enable both on the same function version. Using what each mechanism actually does, explain why they're mutually exclusive and which runtimes get the free option.

Lambda SnapStart and provisioned concurrency both aim to reduce cold-start latency, but they work in different ways and are mutually exclusive because they use different approaches to achieve this goal.

Lambda SnapStart uses cached snapshots of the execution environment to significantly improve startup performance. This means that when a function is invoked, Lambda can immediately reuse a pre-existing snapshot of the execution environment, rather than having to initialize a new one from scratch. This approach is particularly useful for functions that have a high startup time or require a lot of resources to initialize.

On the other hand, provisioned concurrency involves pre-initializing a set of execution environments before they are needed. This allows Lambda to quickly reuse these pre-initialized environments, reducing the time it takes to start a new function invocation. However, this approach requires additional resources and incurs additional charges.

The reason why you can't enable both SnapStart and provisioned concurrency on the same function version is that they use different mechanisms to achieve their goals. SnapStart relies on cached snapshots, while provisioned concurrency relies on pre-initialized execution environments. If both mechanisms were enabled simultaneously, it would create conflicts and inconsistencies in the way Lambda manages function invocations.

As for which runtimes get the free option, it's mentioned in source [3] that when using provisioned concurrency, Lambda initializes the execution environment when you configure the PC settings for a function. This means that functions using provisioned concurrency get the free option, as they don't incur additional charges for the initial execution environment.

In contrast, source [3] also mentions that when using provisioned concurrency, Lambda initializes the execution environment when you configure the PC settings for a function. However, it does not explicitly state which runtime gets the free option.

Because both are alternative solutions to the same cold-start problem, Lambda doesn't allow configuring them together on one function version. SnapStart is available at no extra cost for the Java 11 and Java 17 runtimes, while provisioned concurrency incurs additional charges regardless of runtime.

per_question.question: What's the practical difference between using PutResourcePolicy and AddPermission to grant another service access to invoke your function, and how does that compare to how the execution role's trust policy is scoped?

This allows for more fine-grained control over the permissions granted to other services.

In contrast, when using AddPermission, the permission is granted to the service without any additional conditions or exclusions. This means that the permission is granted to all principals that match the service, without any further filtering or restrictions.

The execution role's trust policy is scoped to the Lambda service principal (lambda.amazonaws.com), which means that only this service is allowed to assume the role and invoke the function. This is different from the PutResourcePolicy and AddPermission approach, where the permission is granted to a specific service (e.g. S3) without any trust policy restrictions.
